body.heading: The three ingredients
paragraphs: Every thunderstorm recipe starts with the same three things: moist air near the ground, unstable air — warm below and cold above — and something to give the warm air a first push upward. A weather front, a hillside, or simply fierce sunshine heating the ground can do it.

Once warm air starts rising, it cools, its moisture condenses into a growing cumulus cloud, and the condensation itself releases heat that fuels more rising. If the conditions are right, the cloud towers into a cumulonimbus that can reach the top of the troposphere, around 12 kilometres up.

body.heading: Where lightning comes from
paragraphs: Inside the storm, ice crystals and soft hail pellets collide in violent updrafts, and the collisions strip electrons from one to the other. Charge builds up — negative toward the cloud’s base, positive toward its top — until the air itself cannot hold the difference.

The discharge is lightning: a channel of air heated hotter than the surface of the Sun in a fraction of a second. Thunder is the sound of that air expanding explosively, arriving at your ears after the flash because sound travels so much more slowly than light.

body.heading: A word on safety
paragraphs: Thunderstorms are beautiful and genuinely dangerous. Lightning can strike well ahead of the rain, so the old rule remains the right one: when thunder roars, go indoors, and wait a good while after the last rumble before heading back out.

takeaway: A thunderstorm is the sky balancing itself — warm, wet air rushing upward, and static electricity snapping back to even things out.
